title: Use genre as a promise, then make the promise your own.
dek: In Chapter 14 of Story, Robert McKee treats genre as a contract with the audience: a familiar pattern of values, conflicts, and emotional movement that gives a story its expectations. The writer's task is to satisfy that contract while finding a distinctive way through it.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: Genre is not a shelf label added after the work is made. It is a promise about the kind of conflict and feeling the audience will receive; learn the promise well enough to keep it, then make your choices distinctive inside it.

canon.heading: Know the promise before you break the pattern.
canon.standfirst: Read the opening section of Chapter 14, "Genre," from Robert McKee's Story on PDF pages 319-343. McKee shows how genre organizes audience expectation through recurring values, conflicts, and emotional experiences, while originality comes from the precise choices made within that frame.
canon.readerIntro: Read this section as a study of audience contract. Mark what the genre promises before the story begins, which values and conflicts define its movement, and where a familiar pattern can become specific rather than formulaic. Then write one genre promise and variation brief for a story, campaign, or product narrative. Stop at PDF page 343.

blocks.label: 01 / Genre is an audience contract
paragraphs: Genre gives the audience a set of expectations about the kind of world, conflict, value change, and emotional experience the story will provide.
Those expectations are not a limitation to evade. They are part of the communication system that lets a new story become legible before every detail is known.

blocks.label: 02 / Choose the genre's central value
paragraphs: A genre is more than a collection of surface devices. Its identity comes from the values it puts under pressure and the kind of change the audience is invited to feel.
Study what moves from positive to negative, or from negative to positive, and the conflicts that make that movement meaningful.

blocks.label: 03 / Familiarity creates room for attention
paragraphs: The audience can spend attention on character, situation, and surprise because genre conventions establish a working map. Without that map, novelty may become confusion rather than interest.
The writer earns freedom by understanding the expectation that a choice is about to confirm, complicate, or overturn.

blocks.label: 04 / Originality lives inside the frame
paragraphs: A story becomes distinctive through its specific world, characters, pressures, and sequence of choices, not through refusing every convention at once.
Use the genre promise as a constraint that sharpens invention: keep the emotional contract clear while making the route to its fulfillment particular to this story.

blocks.label: 05 / Turn the reading into a genre brief
paragraphs: Name the genre, the central value it puts at stake, the audience expectation it creates, and the specific variation your story will introduce.

Stop with one brief that distinguishes a meaningful variation from a decorative twist. The test is whether the audience can recognize the promise and still feel the work has something of its own to say.

closeReading: What does the audience expect to feel or understand before a genre story has supplied its particular details?
Which central value does the genre place under pressure, and how does the story make that value change visible?
When does a convention create useful orientation, and when does repeating it become formula?
Choose one story or brand narrative: what genre promise does it make, and what specific choice makes its execution distinctive?
Write a genre brief naming the promise, central conflict, expected emotional movement, and one meaningful variation.

principle.heading: Use conventions to make originality legible.
principle.body: A familiar form gives the audience a map for attention. Learn the values and emotional movement the form promises, then make the work distinctive through the particular world, pressure, and choices you place inside it.
principle.example: A founder story may use the familiar arc of a difficult problem overcome, but its distinctiveness can come from the unusual customer, constraint, or moral tradeoff that changes what success means.
principle.practice: Choose one story, campaign, or product narrative. Name its genre promise, the value it puts at stake, the emotional movement the audience expects, and one specific choice that makes the work recognizably its own.

output.heading: Make the promise familiar and the route particular.
output.body: Give the audience a clear emotional contract, then earn attention through the specific pressures and choices only this story could contain.

signals.heading: Four current signals on how recognizable promises are becoming the interface for discovery, action, and adoption.

fieldNotes.title: TikTok turns discovery into an explicit commerce promise
fieldNotes.whatHappened: TikTok announced Buy Direct in-app checkout, Shopping Assistant for conversational product guidance, Agentic Leads, a TikTok Ad Network reaching nearly 400,000 apps, and Smart+ tools that combine brand, AI-generated, and creator content in one approval workflow.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The platform is making its promise legible across the whole journey: discover something culturally relevant, understand it in context, and act without leaving the surface. The convention is familiar, but the product is trying to make the route from story to transaction feel native.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether the added automation preserves a distinctive creative point of view, or turns every brand into interchangeable optimized inventory.

fieldNotes.title: Open-weight AI is being sold as a local operating model
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Reflection unveiled Beam, a 501-billion-parameter open-weight model with 23 billion active parameters, a claimed one-million-token context window, and a pitch for institutions to build customized local AI systems on proprietary data. The company's benchmark claims have not been independently verified.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The product story is broader than model capability. It gives enterprises and governments a recognizable genre promise—control your own AI factory—then makes the variation about lower inference cost, local customization, and open distribution.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch the promised weights, technical details, and real deployment evidence; the distinctive story only matters if the operating economics survive contact with production workloads.

fieldNotes.title: ChatGPT ads introduce a visual genre for product discovery
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI announced a visual ad format to be tested during image generation in ChatGPT, with clear labels, expanded conversion measurement, and brand-suitability work with DoubleVerify and Integral Ad Science.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: Advertising is moving into a conversational environment where context is defined by the user's task rather than a page or video. The format has to satisfy the familiar promise of helping people imagine a product while making the new boundary between assistance and persuasion understandable.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether visual ads remain separate from the answer and useful to the decision, or whether the surrounding context makes relevance feel like covert influence.

fieldNotes.title: Safeway brings grocery planning into the assistant itself
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI and Albertsons expanded their partnership so shoppers can start with a recipe, photo, list, or plain-language request in ChatGPT, receive products and savings, build a cart, and move to Safeway for checkout. The companies also describe AI use in recommendations, promotions, and retail workflows.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The familiar shopping promise is being reframed around a decision rather than a catalog: help me make dinner, then carry the plan into a basket. The concrete situation gives the AI experience a genre the shopper already understands.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether task-specific entry points create repeat behavior and trust, especially when recommendations, promotions, and the retailer's commercial interests meet in one conversation.

tweets.author: Yavanika Shah
tweets.title: A product fragment on turning capability into behavior
tweets.summary: This fragment is useful because it names the behavioral question behind a new capability. The important test is not whether the feature is impressive, but whether it changes a repeated workflow enough for the user to adopt it.
tweets.text:
Yes. Switzerland has cheese. Congratulations, everyone. We know.

The slightly more interesting fact is that this is Indian cheese that has actually competed against 1000s of cheeses from around the world and won international awards.

@eleftheriaindia, a Mumbai cheesemaker, had a cheese rank #4 in the world at the 2023 World Cheese Awards, competing against 4,500+ cheeses from 43 countries. It has since picked up more international recognition, including Best Indian Cheese at the 2025 World Cheese Awards in Switzerland.

So maybe, just maybe, the point isn’t “India has better cheese than Switzerland.”

The point is: India makes really bloody good cheese.

And if a PM meeting the Swiss President is an opportunity to put an Indian food business w genuine global credentials in front of Switzerland, why wouldn’t you do it?

We are so used to complaining that India doesn’t market itself, doesn’t build brands, doesn’t export enough cultural soft power etc. And then when someone actually puts an Indian product on the diplomatic table, we’re like:

“BUT SWITZERLAND HAS CHEESE 😭”

Please.

Hatred for the government can survive one cheese basket, guys.

signals.tweetHeading: One fragment from the timeline worth carrying into the work.
